Slide 01
English script

Hello everyone. Today, I will talk about process-trace analysis of iterative decision-making in generative AI-supported art education. My key message is this: non-selected images are learning traces.

上へ
Slide 02
English script

Believe it or not, generative AI has transformed art education. Before AI, students spent more time slowly developing their ideas through sketches. With AI, students can quickly generate many polished images. This creates a new tempo in the classroom.

上へ
Slide 03
English script

We might be surprised by this change, but actually, this kind of transformation has happened before. In this study, we understand AI as one more tool in the history of art education. This is the first part of our research: ART 5.0.

上へ
Slide 04
English script

In the era of ART 5.0, students face several kinds of gaps. We call these discrepancies CAPGAP: cognitive, affective, and participatory gaps. This framework helped us trace our research focus. From there, we identified the CSRI cycle.

上へ
Slide 05
English script

C is for Compare, S is for Select, R is for Review, and I is for Iterate. These four stages help us segment the students’ decision-making flow.

上へ
Slide 06
English script

We examined process traces before the final image. CSRI allows us to segment and observe the flow of students’ decision-making.

上へ
Slide 07
English script

Now, let’s take a look at a short demonstration. While using Canva, students compare images, select one, review it, and try again. This is the CSRI cycle in action.

上へ
Slide 08
English script

Now, let’s take a look at an idea sketch. This is actually an image that the student did not select. The reason was that it felt heavy, too dark, and a bit cluttered.

上へ
Slide 09
English script

Then, the student tried again, and this image was created. Through this interaction, the decision shifted toward a brighter and clearer image that aligned more closely with the student’s intent.

上へ
Slide 10
English script

Here is another non-selected image. The image had many elements, and the focus felt unclear. This shows that rejection can reveal what the student values in the next step.

上へ
Slide 11
English script

This is the selected image from the same case. The student refined the direction through AI outputs and others’ suggestions. The process shows how cognitive, affective, and participatory gaps can shape evaluative decisions.

上へ
Slide 12
English script

Here are the overall results. We analyzed 71 students. Fifty-five students revised their prompts or images. However, only 21 students wrote review notes. Interestingly, 37 students iterated without writing any review notes. This suggests that evaluative decisions may occur even when students do not explicitly record their reflections.

上へ
Slide 13
English script

To conclude, CSRI organized students’ process traces. Unselected images and review notes made evaluative decisions visible. CAPGAP helped us interpret why students revised their ideas. Unselected images are not failures. They are learning traces.
